items.text: CAP theorem: during a network partition, a system must choose between consistency (linearizable reads) and availability (every live node answers). No partition, no forced choice.
CAP is not 'pick any two': partitions happen whether you like it or not, so the real choice is whether the system behaves CP or AP while one is in progress.
PACELC: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Dynamo-style stores are PA/EL; Spanner is PC/EC.
The C in CAP means linearizability, which is unrelated to the C in ACID (transactions preserving application invariants). Same letter, different ideas.
CP vs AP in practice: ZooKeeper and etcd refuse writes on the minority side of a partition; Cassandra and Dynamo-style stores keep accepting writes and reconcile later.
Tunable consistency: Cassandra's per-query consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, ALL) moves each request along the latency vs consistency spectrum.
Linearizability: every operation appears to take effect atomically at one instant between its start and end; once a write completes, every later read sees it.
Sequential consistency: all nodes see operations in one order that respects each process's program order, but that order need not match real time.
Causal consistency: if A could have influenced B, everyone sees A before B. Concurrent, unrelated writes may be seen in different orders on different nodes.
Eventual consistency: if writes stop, all replicas eventually converge. It promises nothing about what reads return in the meantime.
Read-your-writes: after you write, your own later reads reflect it. Implement it by reading from the leader briefly, or by passing a version token replicas must catch up to.
Monotonic reads: a client never sees data go backwards in time. Pin the client to one replica or track the last version it saw.
Monotonic writes: a single process's writes are applied in the order it issued them, on every replica.
Writes-follow-reads: if you read X and then write Y, Y is ordered after X everywhere, so a reply never shows up before the post it answers.
Strict serializability = serializability + linearizability: transactions appear in a single total order that also respects real time. Spanner provides it.
Serializability is about multi-object transactions; linearizability is about single-object recency. A system can offer either one without the other.
Linearizability is expensive: every operation needs coordination, so latency is bounded below by a quorum round trip, which can cross regions.
Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads) combined give causal consistency for a single client session.
Causal consistency is roughly the strongest model that stays available during partitions; anything with real-time ordering, like linearizability, must sacrifice availability.
Consensus: nodes agree on a single value despite failures, with agreement, validity and termination. It underpins leader election, locks and replicated logs.
Majority consensus needs 2f+1 nodes to tolerate f crashed nodes: 3 nodes survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2, 7 survive 3.
Why odd cluster sizes: going from 3 to 4 nodes raises the quorum from 2 to 3 but still tolerates only one failure. You pay for a node and gain nothing.
Paxos roles: proposers suggest values, acceptors vote, learners learn the outcome. A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors accept the same proposal.
Paxos phase 1 (prepare/promise): acceptors promise to ignore proposals numbered below n and report any value already accepted, which the proposer must then adopt.
Multi-Paxos: elect a stable leader and skip phase 1 for later log slots, so each command costs a single round trip to a majority.
Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication and safety, and was explicitly designed to be easier to understand than Paxos.
Raft terms: time is divided into numbered terms with at most one leader each. Any node that sees a higher term immediately reverts to follower.
Raft election: a follower that hears no heartbeat before its election timeout becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself and requests votes from peers.
Raft randomizes election timeouts (e.g., 150-300 ms) so one node usually times out first and wins before others start competing, making split votes rare.
Raft voting rule: a node only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so any elected leader already has every committed entry.
Raft log replication: the leader appends an entry, sends AppendEntries to followers, and marks it committed once a majority have stored it.
Raft log matching: AppendEntries carries the previous entry's index and term; followers reject on mismatch, and the leader backs up until logs agree, then overwrites.
Raft commit subtlety: a leader only commits entries from its own term by counting replicas; earlier-term entries become committed indirectly behind them.
Raft membership changes use joint consensus or one-server-at-a-time changes, so old and new configurations can never form two independent majorities.
Raft log compaction: snapshot the state machine and discard the log prefix; followers that fall too far behind receive the snapshot via InstallSnapshot.
Raft pre-vote: a would-be candidate first checks it could win before bumping its term, so a flapping, partitioned node can't depose a healthy leader.
A single leader caps a consensus group's throughput, so systems run many independent groups, e.g., one Raft group per shard or key range.
Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast): a Paxos-like protocol ensuring all servers deliver updates in the same order, with a recovery phase whenever the leader changes.
Linearizable reads in Raft: a leader must confirm it still leads (ReadIndex heartbeat to a majority) or hold a valid lease, or a deposed leader may serve stale data.
Quorum rule: with N replicas, write to W and read from R. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps the most recent successful write set.
Common quorum setting: N=3, W=2, R=2, which tolerates one unavailable replica for both reads and writes.
Quorum tradeoffs: W=N, R=1 makes reads cheap but one down node blocks writes; W=1, R=N makes writes cheap but one down node blocks reads.
R + W > N alone is not linearizable: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums and partially failed writes can still return stale or flip-flopping values.
Sloppy quorum: when home replicas are unreachable, writes go to any N healthy nodes. Availability rises, but the R + W > N overlap guarantee no longer holds.
Read repair: when a quorum read sees replicas disagree, the coordinator writes the newest value back to the stale replicas.
Majority quorums work because any two majorities of the same N nodes share at least one node, which carries knowledge from one operation to the next.
Lamport clock: increment a counter on each event; on receive, set it to max(local, received) + 1. If A happened-before B, then L(A) < L(B).
Lamport clock limit: L(A) < L(B) does not imply A happened before B. Lamport timestamps cannot detect that two events were concurrent.
Lamport timestamps with node ID as a tiebreaker give a total order over all events that is consistent with causality.
Vector clocks: one counter per node. A happened before B iff A's vector is <= B's in every entry and differs somewhere; if neither dominates, they are concurrent.
Version vectors detect sibling conflicts: Riak can return both concurrent values to the client to merge, instead of silently discarding one.
Hybrid logical clocks (HLC): physical time plus a logical counter, staying close to wall-clock time while preserving causality. Used by CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.
Clock skew: NTP typically keeps servers within milliseconds, but skew can jump to seconds after a bad sync, a VM pause or a misconfigured time source.
Never order cross-machine events by wall-clock timestamps alone: skew between hosts can make an effect appear to happen before its cause.
Last-write-wins silently drops concurrent writes: the higher timestamp survives, even if the other update was the one the user made last.
Use a monotonic clock to measure durations and timeouts; wall-clock time can jump backward or forward when NTP corrects it.
Spanner TrueTime: returns an interval [earliest, latest] with bounded uncertainty, typically a few milliseconds, using GPS receivers and atomic clocks.
Spanner commit wait: after picking commit timestamp s, the leader waits until TrueTime guarantees s is in the past everywhere, yielding external consistency.
Process pauses: a GC pause, VM migration or swapping can freeze a node for seconds, and it resumes acting on leases or beliefs that are no longer true.
Leap seconds have crashed production systems; Google and others 'smear' the extra second over many hours so clocks never repeat or jump.
The 8 fallacies of distributed computing: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, it is secure, topology never changes, one admin, free transport, homogeneous.
Fallacy 'the network is reliable': packets drop, links flap and switches fail, so every remote call needs timeouts, retries and idempotency.
Fallacy 'latency is zero': a cross-region call costs ~100 ms, so a chatty flow with 20 sequential calls takes seconds. Batch and parallelize.
Fallacy 'bandwidth is infinite': moving terabytes between regions takes hours and real money; move computation to the data instead.
A timeout can't tell a dead node from a slow one or a lost reply; the remote side may have executed your request even though you never heard back.
Network partitions are not rare: surveys of production incidents (Bailis and Kingsbury, 2014) found partitions regularly, even inside a single datacenter.
Asymmetric partitions: A can reach B but B can't reach A. One-way links confuse naive heartbeats and can trigger repeated, pointless leader elections.
Geo-distributed consensus: every write needs a majority round trip, so a group spanning continents pays ~100+ ms per commit. Place a majority near the writers.
Failure detectors are inherently unreliable: in an asynchronous network a slow node looks exactly like a crashed one.
Phi accrual failure detector (Cassandra, Akka): outputs a suspicion level based on the observed distribution of heartbeat gaps, instead of a fixed yes/no timeout.
Failure detection tradeoff: short timeouts detect crashes fast but cause false failovers under load spikes; long timeouts leave real failures undetected longer.
SWIM membership: a node pings a random peer; if there's no ack, it asks k other members to ping it indirectly before suspecting it, filtering out one bad link.
Gray failure: a node passes health checks but fails or crawls on real traffic. Detect it from actual request outcomes, not heartbeats alone.
Chandra-Toueg: consensus becomes solvable in an asynchronous system given an unreliable failure detector that is eventually accurate, plus a majority of correct nodes.
Split brain: a partition leaves two nodes each believing it is the leader, both accepting writes and diverging. Majority quorums make this impossible.
Two-node clusters can't form a majority after losing one node. Add a witness or arbiter as a third vote to break ties and avoid split brain.
Fencing token: the lock service issues a monotonically increasing number with each grant, and storage rejects any write carrying a lower token than it has already seen.
Lease: a lock with an expiry. The holder must renew it in time; if the holder dies, the lease simply lapses and another node can take over without manual cleanup.
Leases assume bounded clock drift: the holder should treat its lease as expired slightly early, leaving margin for skew between its clock and the grantor's.
STONITH ('shoot the other node in the head'): before promoting a new leader, forcibly power off or isolate the old one so it can't keep writing.
Redlock debate: Kleppmann argued Redis Redlock is unsafe for correctness because it depends on timing assumptions and issues no fencing tokens. Fine for efficiency locks.
Two-phase commit: the coordinator asks every participant to prepare; if all vote yes it sends commit, otherwise abort. Gives atomic commit across nodes.
2PC blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants vote yes, they must hold locks and wait; none can safely decide commit or abort alone.
A 2PC 'yes' vote is a promise: the participant must durably log the prepare, because it can no longer abort unilaterally, even after a crash.
3PC adds a pre-commit phase so participants can finish without the coordinator, but it assumes bounded network delays and can go wrong under partitions.
2PC over consensus: Spanner makes each participant and the coordinator a Paxos group, so 2PC no longer blocks on the failure of a single machine.
Cost of 2PC: two round trips plus forced log writes at every participant, with locks held throughout, so throughput drops as participants increase.
Saga: a long business transaction split into local transactions, each paired with a compensating action (e.g., refund) that runs in reverse if a later step fails.
Saga orchestration uses a central coordinator that tells each service what to do; choreography has services react to each other's events. Orchestration is easier to trace.
Sagas lack isolation: other transactions can see intermediate states (flight booked, hotel not yet), so use pending states or semantic locks.
Compensation is not rollback: a sent email can't be unsent, so the compensating step is a new corrective action, such as sending a cancellation.
Dual-write problem: updating a DB and publishing to a broker as two separate steps can leave one done and the other not after a crash.
Transactional outbox: write the business row and an outbox event in the same local DB transaction; a relay publishes outbox rows to the broker afterward.
An outbox relay can publish the same event twice (crash after send, before marking it sent), so the outbox gives at-least-once delivery and consumers must dedupe.
Inbox pattern: the consumer records each processed message ID in the same transaction as its side effects, so redelivered messages are detected and skipped.
At-most-once delivery: send without retrying. Messages may be lost but are never duplicated; fine for metrics, wrong for payments.
At-least-once delivery: retry until acknowledged. Nothing is lost but duplicates happen; it's the default for most brokers and requires idempotent consumers.
Exactly-once delivery over a lossy network is impossible; systems offer exactly-once processing, built from at-least-once delivery plus deduplication or atomic commits.
Two Generals problem: over a lossy channel, no finite exchange of messages can make both sides certain they agree to act, so acks alone can't give certainty.
Natural idempotency: 'set balance to 100' is idempotent; 'add 10 to balance' is not. Prefer absolute state updates, or tag each change with a unique operation ID.
Kafka exactly-once: idempotent producers (producer ID + sequence numbers) remove duplicate appends, and transactions commit outputs and consumer offsets atomically.
Dedupe windows: keeping every message ID forever is costly, so systems dedupe within a bounded window; SQS FIFO queues, for example, dedupe over 5 minutes.
CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types): replicas update independently without coordination and are guaranteed to converge when they merge.
State-based CRDT merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas can exchange state in any order, any number of times.
G-Counter CRDT: each replica increments only its own slot; value = sum of slots; merge = element-wise max. It supports increments only.
PN-Counter CRDT: two G-Counters, one for increments and one for decrements; the value is P minus N.
OR-Set (observed-remove set): each add carries a unique tag, and a remove deletes only tags it has observed, so a concurrent add wins over a remove.
Sequence CRDTs (RGA, Logoot, Yjs) give each character a unique, ordered ID, letting concurrent text edits merge without a central server in collaborative editors.
CRDTs guarantee convergence, not business invariants: a CRDT counter can't enforce 'stock never goes below zero' without some coordination.
Gossip protocol: each node periodically shares state with a few random peers; news reaches all N nodes in about O(log N) rounds, like an epidemic.
Gossip is decentralized and robust to node failures, but only eventually consistent. Cassandra uses it to spread membership and node state.
Consistent hashing: nodes and keys hash onto a ring and each key belongs to the next node clockwise, so adding a node moves only ~1/N of keys instead of nearly all of them.
Virtual nodes: each physical node owns many small ring positions, smoothing load imbalance and spreading a failed node's keys across many peers.
Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing: score every node with hash(key, node) and pick the top score. Minimal key movement, no ring to maintain.
Anti-entropy: replicas periodically compare their data in the background and repair differences, catching keys that read repair never touches.
Merkle trees: replicas compare root hashes first and descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ, syncing large datasets while transferring very little.
Hinted handoff: when a replica is down, another node accepts the write with a hint and forwards it once the target comes back.
Hinted handoff is not a durability guarantee: if the node holding the hint also dies, the write never reaches its home replica, so anti-entropy is still required.
Dynamo preference list: a key is stored on the next N distinct physical nodes clockwise on the ring, skipping extra virtual nodes of the same host.
Rack and zone awareness: place replicas in different racks or availability zones so a single power or switch failure can't take out every copy.
Single-leader replication: all writes go to one leader, which streams changes to followers. Simple and well ordered, but the leader caps write throughput.
Multi-leader replication: each datacenter has its own leader for fast local writes, at the cost of resolving conflicts when leaders accept concurrent writes.
Leaderless replication (Dynamo, Cassandra): the client or a coordinator writes to several replicas directly; quorums, read repair and anti-entropy keep them converging.
Failover risk: a promoted async follower may lack the old leader's last writes, and if the old leader comes back, those writes conflict or get discarded.
Failover gone wrong (GitHub, 2012): an out-of-date MySQL follower was promoted and reused auto-increment IDs already referenced in Redis, exposing private data to wrong users.
Chain replication: writes enter at the head and flow down the chain, and reads are served by the tail, giving strong consistency with high throughput.
Statement-based replication breaks on nondeterminism like NOW() or RAND(); row-based (logical) replication ships the actual changed values instead.
Conflict resolution options: last-write-wins, merge with CRDTs, keep siblings for the app to resolve, or avoid conflicts by routing each key's writes to one leader.
Byzantine faults: nodes may lie or send conflicting messages. Tolerating f Byzantine nodes needs 3f+1 nodes, versus 2f+1 for simple crash faults.
PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance) needs O(n^2) messages per decision, which keeps it to small clusters; permissioned ledgers use its descendants.
Most datacenter systems assume crash faults, not Byzantine ones, since one trusted operator runs every node; checksums guard against corruption instead.
FLP impossibility: in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination if even a single process may crash.
Living with FLP: Paxos and Raft are always safe but only guarantee progress when the network behaves well enough, relying on timeouts and randomization.
Partial synchrony: the network may behave arbitrarily badly for a while but eventually delivers messages within some bound. Most consensus proofs assume this model.
Safety vs liveness: safety means nothing bad ever happens (two conflicting commits); liveness means something good eventually happens (a leader is elected).
Tail at scale: if a server has a 1% chance of a slow response, a request fanning out to 100 such servers hits at least one slow reply about 63% of the time.
Hedged requests: send to one replica, and if no reply arrives by about the p95 latency, send a second copy and use whichever answers first. Small extra load, much shorter tail.
Tied requests: send to two replicas at once, each told about the other; whichever starts executing first cancels its twin, limiting duplicate work.
Tail latency sources: GC pauses, background compaction, noisy neighbors, queueing and CPU throttling. You can't eliminate them, so design to tolerate them.
Chandy-Lamport snapshot: marker messages flow through channels so each node records its state plus in-flight messages, capturing a consistent global snapshot without pausing.
Flink exactly-once: checkpoint barriers (Chandy-Lamport style) snapshot all operator state consistently, so after a failure the job rolls back and replays from source offsets.
End-to-end argument: dedupe and integrity checks must ultimately live at the endpoints; TCP's guarantees don't stop your application from processing a request twice.
Partitioning vs replication: partitioning splits data so each node holds a subset (scales capacity); replication copies it (scales reads, survives failures). Most systems do both.
Distributed snapshot reads need a global timestamp: Spanner uses TrueTime, CockroachDB uses HLC, and TiDB uses a central timestamp oracle.
Kafka ISR (in-sync replicas): with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write succeeds only once at least 2 in-sync replicas have it, else the producer gets an error.
Kafka unclean leader election: letting an out-of-sync replica become leader restores availability but loses messages; disabling it favors consistency.
Kafka log compaction keeps at least the latest record per key, turning a topic into a durable changelog that can rebuild a table's current state.
Kafka consumer group rebalancing: partitions are reassigned when consumers join or leave; cooperative (incremental) rebalancing avoids stopping the whole group.
KRaft: modern Kafka replaces ZooKeeper with a built-in Raft metadata quorum, simplifying operations and supporting far more partitions per cluster.
ZooKeeper ephemeral znodes disappear when the creating client's session ends, a natural building block for liveness tracking and leader election.
ZooKeeper lock recipe: each client creates a sequential znode and watches only the one just before it, so releasing the lock wakes one waiter, not a herd.
ZooKeeper writes are linearizable, but reads are served locally by any server and may be stale; call sync() before a read when you need the latest value.
etcd: a Raft-backed key-value store with MVCC revisions, watches and leases. Kubernetes keeps all of its cluster state in it.
etcd watches can resume from a specific revision, so a client never misses changes between listing and watching, unless that revision has been compacted away.
Spanner read-only transactions run lock-free at a snapshot timestamp on any sufficiently up-to-date replica, thanks to TrueTime-assigned commit timestamps.
Dynamo paper (2007): consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, vector clocks, Merkle-tree anti-entropy and gossip, all to keep Amazon's cart always writable.
DynamoDB is not the Dynamo paper design: the service uses leader-based Multi-Paxos replication per partition and offers optional strongly consistent reads.
Cassandra combines Dynamo-style partitioning and replication with a Bigtable-style LSM storage engine, plus tunable consistency on each query.
Chubby: Google's Paxos-based lock service, built for coarse-grained locks held for hours or days, not fine-grained per-request locking.
CockroachDB splits data into ranges (512 MB by default), each replicated by its own Raft group, and runs transactions at serializable isolation by default.
